source.version: Published journal article in Frontiers in Psychology 16:1636906, 08 September 2025; DOI 10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1636906 (p. 1).
source.title_on_document: Why unequal AI access enhances team productivity: the mediating role of interaction processes and cognitive diversity

supplement.holds: Writing task instructions in Section 1 (p. 6, Section 3.3); evaluator instructions and high- and low-scoring sample submissions in Section 2 (p. 7, Section 3.4.2.1); interaction-process coding categories in Section 3 (p. 7, Section 3.4.4). These are descriptions in the main article; the external supplement was not available in the saved PDF. The article does not identify particular numerical results or standard errors as available only in that supplement.

paper_design_summary: A laboratory experiment involved 120 university students in 60 two-person teams, all of whom first wrote a press release without AI; teams were then randomly assigned to a second writing task with either one member or both members allowed to use Kimi (pp. 5–7, Sections 3–3.3 and Figure 3). Marketing professionals rated the team submissions for task quality, with originality also used as an alternative quality measure, and the researchers measured cosine distance between the two teammates’ discussion transcripts (pp. 6–7, Sections 3.4.2–3.4.3; pp. 10–12, Section 4.4.2 and Figure 6). The unequal-versus-full access comparison is randomized, whereas AI-versus-no-AI comparisons use a fixed earlier task with a different product prompt (p. 6, Sections 3 and 3.2–3.3).

studies.label: Laboratory team press-release experiment: unequal versus full AI access, with a common no-AI baseline

assignment.what_was_assigned: Participants were randomly formed into teams, then teams were randomly assigned to unequal or full GenAI access in the treatment phase. In the unequal-access condition, the member receiving AI access was also randomly assigned. Every team completed the no-AI control task first; neither the order nor assignment to a separate no-AI group was randomized (pp. 5–6, Sections 3 and 3.2; p. 7, Figure 3).
assignment.quote: Then, in the treatment phase, these teams were randomly assigned to one of two conditions: only one member could use GenAI (unequal access), or both members could use it (full access).
assignment.locator: p. 6, Section 3, opening paragraph; Section 3.2; p. 7, Figure 3.

arms.name: Unequal AI access
arms.description: Treatment-phase AR-glasses press release: one randomly selected member could use Kimi and the other could not (p. 6, Sections 3.2–3.3). Table 3 reports N = 40 for this condition’s baseline team observations, not a people count (p. 11; p. 10, Section 4.4.1). Per-arm randomized and analyzed people counts are not separately printed.

arms.name: Full AI access
arms.description: Treatment-phase AR-glasses press release: both members could use Kimi (p. 6, Sections 3.2–3.3). Table 3 reports N = 20 for this condition’s baseline team observations, not a people count (p. 11; p. 10, Section 4.4.1). Per-arm randomized and analyzed people counts are not separately printed.

arms.name: No AI access (common first-task baseline)
arms.description: All teams first wrote an electric-bicycle press release without GenAI; this is the shared control phase of the same sample, not an independent randomized arm. Basic document-editing tools were available (p. 6, Sections 3 and 3.2–3.3; p. 7, Figure 3).

participants.exclusions: No exclusions or attrition counts are stated. The paper reports 120 participants, their formation into 60 two-person teams, and 120 rated submissions across the two tasks (pp. 5–7, Sections 3–3.4.2.1). The analyzed people count refers to that stated experimental sample, not Table 1’s regression N or the number of submissions. No separate post-exclusion people total or arm-level people counts are printed. The nine expert raters are not added to the experimental sample.
participants.who: Undergraduate and graduate students from various majors at a university in China, collaborating face to face in two-person teams (pp. 5–6, Sections 3–3.1).
participants.quote: This experiment involved 120 participants, who were made up of undergraduates and graduate students from a university in China.
participants.locator: pp. 5–6, Sections 3–3.1; p. 7, Section 3.4.2.1; p. 11, Table 3 gives baseline team counts of 40 and 20.

ai_tool.name_model: Kimi 3.0, developed by Moonshot, as named in the paper (p. 6, Sections 3 and 3.2).
ai_tool.how_used: Authorized members received a link to Kimi and could interact with it without restrictions while producing the treatment-task press release. Access was restricted to one member or provided to both members according to condition; other websites or applications were prohibited unless instructed (p. 6, Section 3.2).

task.description: Each team collaboratively produced a 700-character Chinese press release using supplied product information: an electric bicycle without AI first, then AR glasses with unequal or full AI access (p. 6, Sections 3.2–3.3).
task.duration: Each writing task should not exceed 45 minutes (p. 6, Section 3.3).

outcomes.name: Expert-rated task quality, including originality-only robustness measure
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Blinded marketing professionals assigned an overall grade from 1 to 7 based on writing quality, content quality, and originality. Nine professionals rated the submissions; each of 120 submissions was assigned to three raters, with each rater evaluating 40 submissions; reported Cronbach alpha = 0.791 (pp. 6–7, Section 3.4.2.1). Coded as usefulness because the main score is explicitly task quality and includes writing/content quality; it is not explicitly a rating of overall creativity. The authors also re-ran the mediation model with originality as the sole quality indicator; this novelty measure is retained here as their stated robustness variant rather than counted as a separate outcome (pp. 10–11, Section 4.4.2; p. 12, Figure 6). Writing quality and content quality are not separately reported outcomes in this PDF. The main OLS analysis reports N = 120 team-task observations (p. 9, Table 1); these are repeated submissions from 60 teams, not 120 independent teams. Prose dispersion labels are preserved as SD, although Figure 4 says its error bars show one standard error.

contrasts.reported: Task quality: unequal access M = 5.654, SD = 0.080; full access M = 5.250, SD = 0.118; t = 2.881, p < 0.01 (p. 8). Table 1, Model (1): Full access to AI b = −0.4023**, adjacent column labeled SD = −2.2771; N = 120. The footnote identifies t statistics and ** p < 0.05; no usable OLS SE is explicitly given (p. 9). Table 3 gives baseline condition Ns of 40 and 20 teams, respectively, not people (p. 11). For the cognitive-diversity indirect pathway, b = −0.283, SE = 0.091, 95% CI [−0.513, −0.134]; for the serial pathway through negative socio-emotional reactions and cognitive diversity, b = −0.061, SE = 0.029, 95% CI [−0.148, −0.021] (p. 9; p. 10, Table 2). Originality-only robustness: cognitive diversity predicts originality, b = 4.619, SE = 1.346, p < 0.01; the corresponding serial indirect effect relative to full access is b = −0.105, SE = 0.050, 95% CI [−0.248, −0.036] (p. 11). These last statistics are mediator associations and indirect effects, not total arm effects on originality. Coefficients retain the paper’s unequal-access reference coding; none is sign-converted or recomputed.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Section 4.1; p. 9, Figure 4A, Table 1 Model (1), Sections 4.2 and 4.3.1; p. 10, Table 2; p. 11, Table 3 and Section 4.4.2; p. 12, Figure 6.

contrasts.reported: Unequal access M = 5.654, SD = 0.080; no access M = 4.981, SD = 0.094; t = −5.103, p < 0.01 (p. 8). Table 1, Model (1): No access to AI b = −0.6730***, adjacent column labeled SD = −5.1990; N = 120. The footnote identifies t statistics and *** p < 0.01 (p. 9). Unequal access is the regression reference. This compares the AI-assisted second task with the shared no-AI first task, with fixed order and different product prompts; it is not a randomized AI-versus-no-AI estimate.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Section 4.1; p. 9, Figure 4A and Table 1 Model (1); p. 6, Sections 3 and 3.2–3.3 establish the non-randomized phase comparison.

outcomes.name: Within-team cognitive diversity of members’ discussion transcripts
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Audio-recorded team discussions were transcribed and manually corrected; all utterances of each member during a task were concatenated, embedded using Universal Sentence Encoder, and normalized. Cognitive diversity is cosine distance between the two teammates’ resulting vectors (p. 7, Section 3.4.3). The produced output scored here is spoken discussion text, not the submitted press release. The measure compares two different people within each team; it does not measure similarity across teams’ final creative products. Robustness models using originality as the quality indicator or difference scores for interaction concentration retain this diversity measure (pp. 11–12, Sections 4.4.2–4.4.3 and Figures 6–7). The main mediation model prints N = 60 (p. 8, Section 4); this is the source for n_units, with the observation-count ambiguity flagged below.

contrasts.reported: Unequal access M = 0.631, SD = 0.011; full access M = 0.510, SD = 0.018; t = 5.938, p < 0.01. Mediation-model coefficient for full access relative to unequal access: b = −0.107, SE = 0.025, p < 0.01 (p. 9). Baseline condition Ns are 40 and 20 teams, respectively (p. 11, Table 3); the mediation model prints N = 60 (p. 8). The SD labels are copied from the prose; Figure 4C’s caption labels its error bars as standard errors. Coefficient signs are preserved in the paper’s reference coding.
contrasts.locator: p. 9, Section 4.2 and Figure 4C; p. 10, Figure 5; p. 8, Section 4, model N; p. 11, Table 3, baseline condition Ns.

contrasts.reported: Unequal access M = 0.631, SD = 0.011; no access M = 0.609, SD = 0.012; t = −1.299, p = 0.197. Mediation-model coefficient for no access relative to unequal access: b = −0.017, SE = 0.020, p > 0.1 (p. 9). The mediation model prints N = 60 (p. 8). This is a fixed-order, different-prompt phase comparison involving the same team sample, not a randomized AI-versus-no-AI contrast.
contrasts.locator: p. 9, Section 4.2 and Figure 4C; p. 10, Figure 5; p. 8, Section 4, model N; p. 6, Sections 3 and 3.2–3.3, phase design.

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine distance d(W_i, W_j) = 1 − cos(W_i, W_j); larger values indicate greater cognitive dissimilarity (p. 7, Section 3.4.3).
diversity_detail.embedding_model: Universal Sentence Encoder (USE) from TensorFlow Hub, citing Cer et al. (2018); a specific model version is not given (p. 7, Section 3.4.3).
diversity_detail.computed_over: One pair of concatenated member-level discussion transcripts within each two-person team for a task. Each member’s utterances across that discussion are combined before embedding; no all-pairs comparison across teams’ final press releases is reported (p. 7, Section 3.4.3).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Independent-sample t-tests compare team cognitive-diversity scores across access conditions (pp. 8–9, Section 4.2). PROCESS mediation-path coefficients have reported SEs (p. 9, Section 4.2); Figure 4C has ±1 standard-error bars (p. 9 caption). The article does not describe a team-clustered or repeated-measures correction for the shared control-phase observations. Bootstrapped confidence intervals in Table 2 concern indirect effects on task quality, not the simple arm difference in diversity (p. 10).
diversity_detail.notes: Retained as computed diversity across two people’s produced discussion texts, with scope flagged because the texts are collaborative process data rather than independently produced final artifacts. No sign reversal is needed for cosine distance. Negative regression coefficients reflect full/no access relative to the unequal-access reference, and are copied without conversion. Prose SD labels conflict with the figure’s SE description; the pooled phase-level observation count is also unclear.

eligibility.reason: The unequal-versus-full AI-access comparison randomly assigns teams to different generative-AI configurations (p. 6, Section 3; Section 3.2). The experiment reports 120 student participants in 60 two-person teams, exceeding the people threshold; these counts are not the number of raters or submissions (pp. 5–7, Sections 3–3.4.2.1). Experts score submitted creative-writing outputs using quality and originality criteria, and originality is also analyzed as a robustness measure (pp. 6–7, Section 3.4.2.1; pp. 10–12, Section 4.4.2 and Figure 6). Core eligibility rests on the randomized ai_design contrast. Comparisons with no AI are fixed-order before–after comparisons with different prompts and do not independently meet criterion 1 (p. 6, Sections 3.2–3.3; p. 14, Section 5.4).

one_line_finding: Unequal AI access produced higher expert-rated press-release quality than full access (M = 5.654 versus 5.250; t = 2.881, p < 0.01; p. 8, Section 4.1) and greater within-team transcript diversity (M = 0.631 versus 0.510; t = 5.938, p < 0.01; p. 9, Section 4.2).
open_questions: Are the dispersions labeled SD in Sections 4.1–4.2 actually standard errors? Figure 4 explicitly defines its bars as ±1 standard error (pp. 8–9). Preserve the printed labels until this is resolved.

Table 1 labels its precision columns SD, including negative values, while its footnote says t statistics in parentheses (p. 9). Obtain unambiguous OLS standard errors before effect extraction; none was derived here.

Clarify the analysis rows and dependence correction: the mediation models print N = 60 (pp. 8 and 11), whereas Table 1 prints N = 120 (p. 9), and the same 60 teams completed both phases (pp. 6–7). The document does not explain a clustering or repeated-measures correction. Per-arm people counts are not separately printed; Table 3’s 40 and 20 are team counts (p. 11).

Does within-team cosine distance between members’ discussion transcripts meet the atlas’s across_people output-diversity scope? It compares different people’s spoken text but not final creative products across independent people or teams (p. 7, Section 3.4.3). This does not affect core eligibility via expert-rated writing outputs.

The external supplement is absent from the saved PDF. Its evaluator instructions may clarify the construction of the overall grade and originality-only score; additional statistics, if any, cannot be confirmed from the main article (pp. 6–7 and 14).
notes: Read the complete markdown through the references; the 16-page PDF has no appended supplement. PDF text was checked for the methods, counts, outcome definitions, results, and declarations; Tables 1–3 were recovered with PyMuPDF, and Figures 3–7 were inspected in memory. One study is recorded because both phases use the same teams. The participant count is the stated 120-person experimental sample; the separate nine-person rater pool is excluded. No per-arm people counts were calculated from team counts. Originality is retained in S1-O1 as the authors’ alternative operationalization of task quality, as required for robustness variants; its reported evidence is an indirect effect, not a printed total treatment effect. Task completion time, communication-process counts/ratios, and self-reported baseline skills are omitted from outcomes because they do not score creative properties or diversity of the produced creative output (pp. 7–8, Sections 3.4.2.2, 3.4.4–3.4.5). There is no unassisted outcome after AI withdrawal; the no-AI task came first (p. 6; p. 7, Figure 3). The data statement promises that raw data will be made available by the authors, without a repository URL; no code URL is stated (p. 14). All reported coefficients and dispersion labels are retained as printed, and no effect sizes or missing standard errors were computed.
